Bayesian Variance of a Fit

Source: R/inference_objects.R
bayesian_vcov.Rd

Selects the variance \(V_b = (H + S)^{-1}\), the inverse of the penalized information: the information \(H\) of the log-likelihood plus the second derivative \(S\) of the penalty. It is the posterior variance under the prior whose negative logarithm is the penalty, conditional on the hyperparameters, and it is the default of every function that takes a vcov_type.

Usage

bayesian_vcov(information = NULL)

Arguments

information

NULL (the default) or the matrix \(H\), an object that inherits from distributions7::Information:

  • NULL: the matrix is chosen for each fit by the family of the fit, as distributions7::observed_info() where the log-likelihood is twice differentiable in every parameter of the family (every distributions7::params_order() is at least 2), and as distributions7::expected_info() with method = NULL, for the whole matrix, otherwise. The families with a kink in a parameter, such as the Laplace, have a singular observed information in that parameter and take the expected one;

  • distributions7::observed_info(): the negative Hessian of the log-likelihood at the data;

  • distributions7::expected_info(): the Fisher information, whose method is NULL (the closed form of the family where it has one, distributions7::expect_opg() otherwise) or one of distributions7::expect_opg(), distributions7::expect_integrate() and distributions7::expect_mc() (see distributions7::expected_derivative_methods).

auto_info() is not accepted. A model with a structural term is inverted on the observed information whatever the object says. The choice does not depend on how the fit was computed (inner_information of statmod()). summary.StatmodFit() states the matrix when it is not the observed one, and a printed variance object states the information that it names. information_objects compares the objects.

Value

A BayesianVcov object, inheriting from vcov_method, with the property name equal to "bayesian" and the property information.

Details

Choose it for an interval around a penalized term: it carries the smoothing bias as variance, and such intervals cover at about their nominal rate. It does not include the uncertainty of the hyperparameters, for which unconditional_vcov() is the convention. See vcov_method for the three side by side and vcov.StatmodFit() for the matrices in full.

See also

frequentist_vcov() and unconditional_vcov() for the siblings, vcov_method for the comparison, and vcov.StatmodFit(), confint.StatmodFit(), summary.StatmodFit() and statmod_test() for the functions that take it.

Examples

set.seed(1)
dd <- data.frame(x = runif(80))
dd$y <- 1 + 2 * dd$x + rnorm(80, sd = 0.4)
fit <- statmod(y ~ x, distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), dd)
bayesian_vcov()
#> <vcov> bayesian
vcov(fit, vcov_type = bayesian_vcov())
#>                   mu:(Intercept)          mu:x sigma:(Intercept)
#> mu:(Intercept)      7.691473e-03 -1.161719e-02      1.055974e-18
#> mu:x               -1.161719e-02  2.209835e-02     -2.501978e-18
#> sigma:(Intercept)   1.055974e-18 -2.501978e-18      6.410256e-03
confint(fit, vcov_type = bayesian_vcov())
#>                   parameter   term coefficient  estimate         se      lower
#> mu:(Intercept)           mu linpar (Intercept)  1.043291 0.08770104  0.8714004
#> mu:x                     mu linpar           x  2.007856 0.14865515  1.7164973
#> sigma:(Intercept)     sigma linpar (Intercept) -1.032801 0.08006408 -1.1897235
#>                        upper
#> mu:(Intercept)     1.2151822
#> mu:x               2.2992148
#> sigma:(Intercept) -0.8758781

# the standard errors from the expected information instead
vcov(fit, vcov_type = bayesian_vcov(
  information = distributions7::expected_info()))
#>                   mu:(Intercept)        mu:x sigma:(Intercept)
#> mu:(Intercept)       0.007691473 -0.01161719       0.000000000
#> mu:x                -0.011617186  0.02209835       0.000000000
#> sigma:(Intercept)    0.000000000  0.00000000       0.006410256
